taxonomyNote: NatureServe lists the species as Haldea striatula (genus resurrected by McVay and Carstens 2013); the Missouri Department of Conservation lists it as Virginia striatula, 'formerly Haldea striatula', so the source genus disagrees in direction.
fieldMarks: Small, plain, secretive snake, 7-10 in, uniform gray, brown or reddish-brown with an unmarked cream or light-gray belly.
Strongly keeled back scales (feels rough), 5 upper-lip scales, a single scale between the nostrils and one postocular scale touching the eye; anal plate usually divided.
Differs from the smooth earth snake by five supralabials, usually one preocular and keeled dorsal scales.
behavior: Semifossorial and seldom above ground; hides under logs, flat rocks and leaf litter and may be active at night in warm, damp weather.
Eats mainly earthworms, occasionally slugs, snails, small frogs and lizards.
Active March-October (late March to early November in Missouri); young 2-13 per litter are born live in late July-September.
habitat: Rocky hillsides of dry open woods, cedar glades, woodland edges, pastures, wooded bottomlands, hammocks, pine flatwoods, gardens and vacant urban lots, where moisture and cover occur.
range: Southeastern and south-central United States: Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri (Ozarks), Mississippi, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Virginia; not in Canada.
